summary: Jesus turns from farewell speech to prayer. He asks the Father to glorify the Son so the Son may glorify the Father and give eternal life, defined as knowing the Father and Jesus Christ whom he sent. He prays for the disciples' protection, joy, sanctification, and mission, then for future believers whose unity and love are to make his sending visible to the world.
whyItMatters: The prayer lets readers overhear the relationships that ground John's theology: glory as self-giving, eternal life as knowledge, holiness as consecration for mission, and unity as participation in Father and Son. Jesus does not pray for escape from the world but for a protected, truthful, sent people within it.

context.author: The anonymous Fourth Gospel narrator, bringing the farewell discourse to its theological climax in Jesus's prayer
context.audience: The first disciples and later believers drawn into the prayer through their testimony
context.date: Prayed immediately before the arrest in John's narrative
context.setting: The transition from the farewell setting toward the garden across the Kidron
context.literaryForm: Intercessory prayer moving from Son and Father, to present disciples, to future believers and the world

outline.heading: The Son asks for glory and defines eternal life
Jesus prays for disciples given from the world
Protection, joy, truth, sanctification, and sending
Future believers, unity, witness, glory, and love

keyVerses.text: This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.
keyVerses.why: Eternal life is personal participation in knowing the Father through the sent Son, not merely endless duration.

keyVerses.text: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.
keyVerses.why: The community is consecrated for mission through the Father's revealed reality.

keyVerses.text: that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
keyVerses.why: Christian unity participates in divine communion and serves public witness.

questions.question: Is this prayer called ‘high priestly’ in the text?
questions.answer: John never supplies that title. Christian interpreters have long called it Jesus's ‘high-priestly prayer’ because he consecrates himself, intercedes for his people, and approaches death. The label can illuminate, but readers should first hear the prayer's own vocabulary—glory, giving, name, keeping, truth, sending, unity, and love.

questions.question: How is the cross ‘glory’?
questions.answer: Jesus says the hour has come and asks the Father to glorify the Son so the Son may glorify the Father. In John, crucifixion, resurrection, and return form one ‘lifting up’: the cross reveals divine self-giving rather than contradicting glory. The Son's completed obedience makes the Father's character known, and the Father vindicates the Son.

questions.question: What does ‘know’ mean in the definition of eternal life?
questions.answer: Ginōskō can describe knowledge gained in relationship and experience, not bare awareness of propositions. Eternal life is knowing the only true God and the one he sent. This includes truthful confession, but it is participatory and covenantal: Jesus has made the Father's name known, and disciples have received the words and recognized his mission.

questions.question: Why does Jesus say he is not praying for the world?
questions.answer: At this point Jesus distinguishes his immediate intercession for the disciples given to him; he is not declaring that the world lies outside God's love. The Gospel says God loves the world, Jesus is its Savior, and the prayer soon asks that the world believe and know. Focused prayer for endangered witnesses serves the wider mission to the world.

questions.question: What does keeping disciples in the Father's ‘name’ mean?
questions.answer: A divine name represents revealed identity and authority, not a protective sound. Jesus has manifested the Father's name by making the Father known and asks that disciples be guarded within that reality. Their unity is therefore grounded in shared belonging to God, not in suppressing difference through institutional force.

questions.question: Does Jesus ask believers to withdraw from the world?
questions.answer: He explicitly does not ask that the Father remove them, but protect them from the evil one. ‘Not of the world’ describes the source and allegiance of their life; ‘sent into the world’ describes their location and vocation. Holiness in this prayer is missional presence rather than social disappearance or contempt for creation.

questions.question: What does sanctification in truth involve?
questions.answer: Hagiazō means make holy, consecrate, or set apart for God's purpose. The Father sanctifies disciples in truth, and Jesus sanctifies himself—consecrates himself to death—so they may be truly consecrated. Because this sits between protection and sending, holiness is formation by God's word for faithful mission, not mere isolation or moral superiority.

questions.question: What kind of unity does Jesus pray for?
questions.answer: Its model is the differentiated mutual indwelling of Father and Son, not sameness or absorption. The unity carries visible purpose: so the world may believe and know the Father sent Jesus and loved the disciples. Organizational reconciliation can serve that witness, but unity also demands shared truth, received glory, practiced love, and communion ‘in us.’

glossary.def: To know, often with relational and experiential force rather than mere awareness.
To sanctify, make holy, or consecrate for God's purpose.
God's character made visible; in John supremely revealed and vindicated through Jesus's ‘hour.’
